reasoning: 1. TARGET ENGAGEMENT: No biomarker data available to confirm nilotinib engaged BCR-ABL. However, nilotinib is a well-established BCR-ABL inhibitor with known pharmacology, so target engagement is likely but unconfirmed in this trial. 2. PATHWAY MODULATION: No pathway biomarkers reported to assess whether kinase inhibition occurred downstream of BCR-ABL engagement. 3. CLINICAL TRANSLATION: Primary endpoint clearly failed - 4-month PFS rate was only 27% in no CNS mets cohort and 12.5% in CNS mets cohort, both well below typical efficacy thresholds for melanoma trials. PFS was also short at 3.4 and 2.4 months respectively. 4. POPULATION EFFECTS: Clear difference between CNS and no-CNS metastases subgroups, with no-CNS cohort performing better (27% vs 12.5% 4-month PFS rate, 2 partial responses vs 0). This suggests the mechanism may have some activity in the no-CNS population but insufficient for clinical benefit. 5. CONFOUNDERS: Small sample size (N=20) but this appears adequately powered for a Phase 2 single-arm trial. No obvious confounders - this appears to be a straightforward test of whether BCR-ABL inhibition works in melanoma.

failure_modes.evidence: Nilotinib targets BCR-ABL, which is the hallmark oncogene of CML and some ALL cases. Melanoma typically lacks BCR-ABL fusion proteins, making this population mechanistically inappropriate for a BCR-ABL inhibitor. The trial enrolled 'TKI resistant or intolerant patients with metastatic mucosal, acral, or chronically sun damaged melanoma' but provided no evidence that these melanomas harbored BCR-ABL alterations.
